text: Three tools that all exist to move and transform data — not competitors doing unrelated things, but three real generations of the same underlying job, each one aimed at a different era of infrastructure.

SSIS is the oldest: a Windows-based, on-premises ETL engine tied to a SQL Server license, still genuinely the right call for organizations with deep on-premises investments. Azure Data Factory is a cloud platform-as-a-service you configure and manage yourself — stable, hybrid-capable, and still the right call for most existing production pipelines today. Fabric Data Factory is a cloud software-as-a-service built directly into a Fabric workspace, alongside lakehouses and Power BI — and it's where Microsoft is actively investing new development.

Fabric keeps roughly ninety percent of ADF's activities, and pipelines, activities, and triggers all transfer directly. But it isn't perfect yet. There's currently no equivalent to ADF's Azure-SSIS integration runtime, so organizations with real SSIS package dependencies can't move them over. And managed virtual networks and private endpoints are still officially listed as to be determined.

So how do you actually choose? A mature on-premises SQL Server shop already running SSIS packages should keep using SSIS — migrating working packages for its own sake rarely pays off. An existing, stable hybrid pipeline already built in ADF should generally stay there. And a brand-new, cloud-native project with no legacy dependency is genuinely where Microsoft recommends starting with Fabric today.

Same underlying job, three different tools for three different moments in a real organization's history — and knowing which one a project actually calls for is itself part of the skill. Next: getting hands-on and actually creating a real Data Factory instance in the Azure portal.
